claims.text: Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking and limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
High-pressure, high-temperature treatment in a hexahedron-anvil apparatus will refine the dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The treatment will make the microstructure more homogeneous.
The treatment will reduce deleterious internal boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
A suitable pressure-temperature regime can induce controlled recrystallization and refinement without erasing the lamellar-colony architecture.
High-pressure, high-temperature treatment will promote recovery and controlled recrystallization.
Recovery and controlled recrystallization will heal or modify internal boundaries that act as microcrack-nucleation sites.
Modification of the internal boundaries will reduce local stress concentrations.
The treatment may enable beneficial precipitation or dislocation-structure adjustments.
Precipitation hardening and microstructural refinement will increase alloy strength.
Suppressing microcrack initiation at internal boundaries will increase room-temperature tensile ductility.
Relative to the untreated baseline, treated samples will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength.
Relative to the untreated baseline, treated samples will exhibit a statistically significant increase in room-temperature tensile ductility.
Treated samples will have fewer microcrack-initiation sites than untreated samples.
Complete phase homogenization or degradation of the lamellar colonies defines an upper processing boundary beyond which the intervention is not expected to be effective.
Effectiveness may be limited to compositions and processing histories typical of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The optimal pressure, temperature, and duration are uncertain and require experimental calibration.
The balance between strength and ductility improvements may vary with composition and processing history.
